tools.name: AskUserQuestion
tools.description:
Use this tool only when you are blocked on a decision that is genuinely the user's to make: one you cannot resolve from the request, the code, or sensible defaults.

Usage notes:
- Users will always be able to select "Other" to provide custom text input
- Use multiSelect: true to allow multiple answers to be selected for a question
- If you recommend a specific option, make that the first option in the list and add "(Recommended)" at the end of the label

Plan mode note: To switch into plan mode, use EnterPlanMode (not this tool). Once in plan mode, use this tool to clarify requirements or choose between approaches BEFORE finalizing your plan. Do NOT use this tool to ask "Is my plan ready?", "Should I proceed?", or otherwise reference "the plan" in questions — the user cannot see the plan until you call ExitPlanMode for approval.

Reserve this for decisions where the user's answer changes what you do next — not for choices with a conventional default or facts you can verify in the codebase yourself. In those cases pick the obvious option, mention it in your response, and proceed.

Preview feature:
Use the optional `preview` field on options when presenting concrete artifacts that users need to visually compare:
- ASCII mockups of UI layouts or components
- Code snippets showing different implementations
- Diagram variations
- Configuration examples

Preview content is rendered as markdown in a monospace box. Multi-line text with newlines is supported. When any option has a preview, the UI switches to a side-by-side layout with a vertical option list on the left and preview on the right. Do not use previews for simple preference questions where labels and descriptions suffice. Note: previews are only supported for single-select questions (not multiSelect).

questions.description: Questions to ask the user (1-4 questions)

question.description: The complete question to ask the user. Should be clear, specific, and end with a question mark. Example: "Which library should we use for date formatting?" If multiSelect is true, phrase it accordingly, e.g. "Which features do you want to enable?"

header.description: Very short label displayed as a chip/tag (max 12 chars). Examples: "Auth method", "Library", "Approach".

options.description: The available choices for this question. Must have 2-4 options. Each option should be a distinct, mutually exclusive choice (unless multiSelect is enabled). There should be no 'Other' option, that will be provided automatically.

label.description: The display text for this option that the user will see and select. Should be concise (1-5 words) and clearly describe the choice.

preview.description: Optional preview content rendered when this option is focused. Use for mockups, code snippets, or visual comparisons that help users compare options. See the tool description for the expected content format.

multiSelect.description: Set to true to allow the user to select multiple options instead of just one. Use when choices are not mutually exclusive.

answers.description: User answers collected by the permission component

annotations.description: Optional per-question annotations from the user (e.g., notes on preview selections). Keyed by question text.

preview.description: The preview content of the selected option, if the question used previews.

notes.description: Free-text notes the user added to their selection.

metadata.description: Optional metadata for tracking and analytics purposes. Not displayed to user.

source.description: Optional identifier for the source of this question (e.g., "remember" for /remember command). Used for analytics tracking.

tools.name: Bash
tools.description:
Executes a bash command and returns its output.

- Working directory persists between calls, but prefer absolute paths — `cd` in a compound command can trigger a permission prompt. Shell state (env vars, functions) does not persist; the shell is initialized from the user's profile.
- IMPORTANT: Avoid using this tool to run `cat`, `head`, `tail`, `sed`, `awk`, or `echo` commands, unless explicitly instructed or after you have verified that a dedicated tool cannot accomplish your task. Instead, use the appropriate dedicated tool as this will provide a much better experience for the user.

tools.name: ScheduleWakeup
tools.description:
Schedule when to resume work in /loop dynamic mode — the user invoked /loop without an interval, asking you to self-pace iterations of a specific task.

Do NOT schedule a short-interval wakeup to poll for background work you started — when harness-tracked work finishes, you are re-invoked automatically, so polling is wasted. Instead schedule a long fallback (1200s+) so the loop survives if the work hangs or never notifies. The exception is external work the harness cannot track (a CI run, a deploy, a remote queue) — there, pick a delay matched to how fast that state actually changes.

Pass the same /loop prompt back via `prompt` each turn so the next firing repeats the task. For an autonomous /loop (no user prompt), pass the literal sentinel `<<autonomous-loop-dynamic>>` as `prompt` instead — the runtime resolves it back to the autonomous-loop instructions at fire time. (There is a similar `<<autonomous-loop>>` sentinel for CronCreate-based autonomous loops; do not confuse the two — ScheduleWakeup always uses the `-dynamic` variant.) To end the loop, call this tool with `stop: true` (omit every other field) — the loop ends immediately and no further wakeups fire.

Set `noop: true` if nothing changed — you checked and there's nothing to report ("no change", "still waiting", "quiet hold"). Set `noop: false` if something happened worth keeping — you edited a file, posted a message, advanced state, or surfaced a finding. Consecutive `noop: true` ticks are collapsed in the user's terminal view and tracked as a streak, so long quiet holds stay legible to the user without scrolling. Omit `noop` when stopping (`stop: true`).

## Picking delaySeconds

This session's requests use a 1-hour Anthropic prompt-cache TTL, so effectively every allowed delay (the runtime clamps to [60, 3600]) wakes up with your conversation context still cached. There is no cache cliff inside that range to pace around, and scheduling extra wakeups just to keep the cache warm is pure waste — never do that. (If the session enters usage overage, later requests drop to the 5-minute TTL; don't try to track or preempt that — the guidance here stays the same.)

Match the delay to what you're actually waiting for:

- **Actively polling external state the harness can't notify you about** (a CI run, a deploy, a remote queue): pick the delay from how fast that state actually changes. A CI run that takes ~8 minutes deserves one ~480s check, not eight 60s ones.
- **The long fallback heartbeat** (something else — a Monitor, a task notification — is the primary wake signal): 1200s+, so quiet wakeups stay rare.
- **Idle ticks with no specific signal to watch**: default to **1200s–1800s** (20–30 min). The loop still checks back regularly, and the user can always interrupt if they need you sooner.

Don't think in cache windows — think about what you're actually waiting for.

## The reason field

One short sentence on what you chose and why. Goes to telemetry and is shown back to the user. "watching CI run" beats "waiting." The user reads this to understand what you're doing without having to predict your cadence in advance — make it specific.

tools.name: SendFeedback
tools.description:
Use this tool to draft feedback about Claude Code when you hit a high-signal moment. That includes both PRODUCT issues and MODEL-BEHAVIOR issues:
- a reproducible tool or product failure was just resolved or abandoned
- the user clearly expressed frustration with Claude Code or with how you handled the task
- you hit a missing capability that blocked a reasonable request
- you notice, or the user points out, that your own behavior in this session went wrong, for example: you gave a confident answer then had to retract it; you stopped short and handed work back when you could have finished; you declined or disputed a reasonable request; you spawned more subagents than the task warranted; your tone was off; you asked more clarifying questions than needed; you expanded scope beyond what was asked

The draft is QUEUED LOCALLY. It is never sent without the user's explicit approval, and calling this tool renders no UI and does not interrupt the conversation, so never announce it or ask the user about it mid-task.

Write `details` as short labeled bullets in this exact order, one to three lines each, no narrative paragraphs:
- **What happened:** the observed behavior vs. what was expected, with exact error text if short. Facts only.
- **What the user said:** the user's own words that prompted this, quoted. If nothing did, write "User didn't comment; observed by the model." Never paraphrase sentiment into a stronger claim.
- **Repro:** the minimal steps or shape that reproduces it.
- **Evidence:** identifiers a reader can chase, such as request IDs, timestamps, file paths, versions. Omit the bullet if there are none.

Constraints:
- Never fabricate or exaggerate user sentiment; report only what actually happened.
- Everything in the draft must be sourced from the user or the session, never inferred: leave unknown fields blank rather than guess, and add a final **Cause:** bullet only for a root cause you verified in-session.
- Use `area` to name the part of Claude Code the feedback is about (a feature, command, or workflow, e.g. "hooks config", "/help", "file editing") when there is a clear one; leave it blank otherwise.
- Use `failure_mode` ONLY when the report is about model behavior (how Claude responded), not a product bug. Pick the single closest value, or `other` when it is a model-behavior issue that fits no listed value; omit the field only when the report is a product/tool bug with no model-behavior component.
- Use `task_category` to name what kind of task the session was doing, or `other` when it is a clear task that fits no listed value. Omit only if genuinely unclear.
- Do not include secrets or credentials. Refer to people by role ("a teammate", "the PR reviewer"), never by name, email address, or chat/user ID. This applies inside quoted user words too: replace a name or handle with a bracketed role (e.g. "[a teammate]") and keep the rest verbatim. Do not include customer-facing channel or DM IDs, or excerpts of customer content. Session, request, and run IDs, timestamps, repo/PR numbers, and file paths (written relative to the working directory, or ~-prefixed, not absolute paths under the user's home) remain the right evidence.
- If the issue looks like a security vulnerability: describe the class of problem, never a working exploit or step-by-step extraction path.
- Draft only at the natural moments listed above, and at most one draft per distinct issue; never re-draft the same issue in a session.

tools.name: Skill
tools.description:
Invoke a skill.

A skill is a packaged set of instructions the user or project has set up for a particular kind of task (deploy steps, a review checklist, a repo-specific workflow). Available skills appear in a system-reminder listing with one-line descriptions. When the task at hand is one a listed skill covers, call this tool first — the skill's instructions load into the turn for you to follow in place of your default approach; some skills instead run in a subagent and return the finished result. A skill that runs in the background returns only the agent's name — its result arrives later as a task notification, so don't wait on it or invoke it again in the meantime. Users may also ask for one by name (`/<name>`, or "slash command"); that's a request to invoke it.

- `skill`: exact name from the listing, no leading slash. Plugin skills use `plugin:skill`. Directory-scoped skills are listed with a path prefix (`apps/web:deploy`); when both scoped and unscoped variants of a name exist, pick the one whose directory contains the files you're working on (most specific wins; unscoped otherwise).
- `args`: optional arguments to pass through.

Only names from the listing (or that the user typed explicitly) are valid. Built-in CLI commands (`/help`, `/clear`, …) aren't skills. If a `<command-name>` block is already present this turn, the skill is loaded — follow it directly rather than calling again.

tools.name: ToolSearch
tools.description:
Fetches full schema definitions for deferred tools so they can be called.

Deferred tools appear by name in <system-reminder> messages. Until fetched, only the name is known — there is no parameter schema, so the tool cannot be invoked. This tool takes a query, matches it against the deferred tool list, and returns the matched tools' complete JSONSchema definitions inside a <functions> block. Once a tool's schema appears in that result, it is callable exactly like any tool defined at the top of the prompt.

Result format: each matched tool appears as one <function>{"description": "...", "name": "...", "parameters": {...}}</function> line inside the <functions> block — the same encoding as the tool list at the top of this prompt.

Query forms:
- "select:Read,Edit,Grep" — fetch these exact tools by name
- "notebook jupyter" — keyword search, up to max_results best matches
- "+slack send" — require "slack" in the name, rank by remaining terms

tools.name: Workflow
tools.description:
Execute a workflow script that orchestrates multiple subagents deterministically. Workflows run in the background — this tool returns immediately with a task ID, and a <task-notification> arrives when the workflow completes. Use /workflows to watch live progress.

ONLY call this tool when the user has explicitly opted into multi-agent orchestration. Workflows can spawn dozens of agents and consume a large amount of tokens; the user must request that scale, not have it inferred. Explicit opt-in means one of:
- The user included the keyword "ultracode" in their prompt (you'll see a system-reminder confirming it).
- Ultracode is on for the session (a system-reminder confirms it) — see **Ultracode** in the workflow authoring reference.

- The user asked you to run a specific named or saved workflow.

For any other task — even one that would clearly benefit from parallelism — do NOT call this tool. Use the Agent tool (if available) for individual subagents, or briefly describe what a multi-agent workflow could do and how much it would roughly cost, and ask the user whether to run it. 1	# vc-x1-messages v0.3.3
2	
3	Messages for the vc-x1 family. The open threads are the inbox, the history is the archive.
4	
5	One shared repo every participant can reach is the only thing the protocol assumes. A thread is
6	one file, appended by everyone who takes part in it, so reading a conversation is reading one
7	file, and a search for a message's id returns everything ever said under it. Every member's
8	`custom.md` points at this file, and taking part means following it, pushes included.
9	
10	## Terminology
11	
12	Each term stands alone, a term that relies on another follows it, and a kind of a term sits
13	under it.
14	
15	- **Member**: a participant, named by its project's name, `vc-x1`, `iiac-perf`, `zc-ring-x1`.
16	- **Thread**: one conversation, the file `open/m-<tid>.md` while open and `closed/m-<tid>.md`
17	  after, headed `# m-<tid> <title>`, each of its lines an `m-<tid>-<num>`, so `rg -w m-<tid>`
18	  returns the whole thread. The directory is the thread's state, and any member may write a line
19	  in any open thread.
20	- **Thread id**: `<tid>`, an integer, never reused.
21	  - Its store is the tracked file `threads`, one integer, the last id issued, never decreased.
22	  - The opener reads it, adds one, writes it back, and takes the new value, in the opening commit.
23	- **Title**: the opener's, a few words, never changed.
24	- **Line**: one message or mark, one physical line, always, appended oldest first directly
25	  under the heading, no blank line anywhere in the file:
26	  `- m-<tid>-<num> <time> from <author> <action> <info>`.
27	- **Number**: `<num>`, an integer from 0, one more than the last line in the file, so the thread
28	  is its own counter and nothing else stores it: line `<num>` is file line `<num>` plus two, and
29	  the next number is the file's line count less one. Every `m-<tid>-<num>` is unique and the numbers
30	  order the thread, so a search for one returns the line and every later line that names it. An
31	  id, thread or line, is final once written, since one clone mints them (see What is not here),
32	  and a rejected push, which only a second clone causes, renumbers before pushing again.
33	- **Time**: when the line was written, UTC to the second, `2026-09-09T16:05:42Z`. For a human
34	  reading the thread, never for ordering, as clocks may not agree.
35	- **Author**: the member who wrote the line, after the word `from`, which is there for the human
36	  eye, since the position already says it.
37	- **Action**: what the line does, one of two:
38	  - **`to`**: a message. Info is the recipients, comma-joined with no spaces, a space, then the
39	    text. A recipient need not have been in the thread before, so a forward is a `to` naming the
40	    new member and saying what is forwarded. A reply begins its text with the id it answers when
41	    position alone would leave that ambiguous, as in a thread of three.
42	  - **`done`**: a mark, no info. The author has nothing to say to the lines before it. Any line
43	    from a member clears what was pending for them, so this is the line for when there is
44	    nothing else to write, and the closer's last word.
45	- **Info**: the message text, or its title and a message-link to its body,
46	  `[<title>](m-<tid>-<num>.md)`, relative to the thread's own directory so the link survives
47	  the close.
48	- **Body**: `m-<tid>-<num>.md` beside its thread, for a message that wants more than a line. It
49	  begins `# m-<tid>-<num> <title>`, so a search for the id finds it and the heading is an anchor,
50	  and it ends at the end of the file. Full markdown inside, headings, lists, and code blocks, and
51	  a quoted line is inert since a body is never read for lines. Moved with its thread.
52	- **Addressed**: a member is addressed by every `to` line naming them in its recipient field,
53	  and by nothing else. A member named in a line's text or in a body is referenced, never
54	  addressed, so a tool computing pending reads the recipient field, not the whole line.
55	- **Pending**: for a member, every `to` line naming them numbered above their latest line in
56	  that thread, of either action, all of them when they have written none. Their open
57	  obligations, and what Read messages returns: a line stays pending until they write after it,
58	  however many times it has been read, and a later line naming them makes them pending again.
59	  So a reply is its author's own clearance, and a question back puts the ball in the other
60	  court until the answer comes.
61	- **Complete**: every addressed member has a line numbered above every `to` line naming them.
62	  Computed from the file alone.
63	- **Closed**: the file is under `closed/`, moved there whole with its bodies, so every thread
64	  ever is in the tree, in this file's shape, and a reader parses one shape. History is
65	  provenance, never a store. A closed thread takes no line, and a late thought opens a new
66	  thread naming the old id.
67	- **Message-link**: a live link within this repo, `[<text>](<file>#<slug>)`, relative to the
68	  linking file and resolving to whatever the reader's checkout holds. The form for a body.
69	- **Sha-link**: a URL naming a commit SHA (`blob/<sha>/<path>#<slug>`), never a branch, which
70	  moves or dies. The form for content in another repo, where only a commit is durable.
71	- **Clone**: one, on one machine, one owner at a time, since the ids are allocated under its
72	  mutex (see What is not here). `owner` (gitignored) holds `<time> take|release <member>` lines,
73	  the time in a line's form, UTC to the second, and the last line names the owner. It is not a
74	  dotfile, so an `ls` shows who holds the clone.
75	- **Take ownership**: append a `take` line to `owner`. Yours until released. A `take` with no
76	  `release` after it means a session is writing, or died writing, and only a human tells the two
77	  apart and clears the second by writing the release.
78	- **Release ownership**: rewrite `owner` to the one `release` line, so the file holds at most
79	  the last release and the current take, and never grows. The clone is free.
80	
81	## Read Actions
82	
83	### Read messages
84	
85	This is a read only action, no ownership and no fetch.
86	
87	1. For each thread file, `open/m-<tid>.md` and never a body `open/m-<tid>-<num>.md`, find the
88	   `to` lines naming you. One numbered above your latest line in that file is pending, and the
89	   thread is the context to read it in.
90	2. Nothing pending, and `owner` shows no owner: consider doing a Fetch.
91	
92	A tool may do the search. The rule is the file, and the tool is a convenience.
93	
94	### Find a thread
95	
96	Every thread is in the tree, under `open/` or `closed/`.
97	
98	- Titles: `head -1 open/*.md closed/*.md`. Titles and openers: `head -2`.
99	- One thread: `cat open/m-<tid>.md` or `cat closed/m-<tid>.md`, `rg -w m-<tid>` for both and
100	  its bodies.
101	- A thread's commits, each titled with the thread ids it touched:
102	  `git log --oneline -- open/m-<tid>.md closed/m-<tid>.md`.
103	
104	## Write Actions
105	
106	Every write runs inside these guards, in order:
107	
108	- `Read messages` first, so the write answers the traffic as it stands.
109	- Read `owner`: no other member has taken ownership.
110	- Any guard failing: show the user and ask how to proceed.
111	- Re-read `owner` before releasing, and a `take` after yours means stop and show both lines.
112	- A rejected push: work with the user to correct the situation.
113	
114	Every write is an append: a thread file grows at its end, a body is a new file, and `threads` is
115	the one value that is overwritten. Nothing edits a line or a body once written.
116	
117	1. Take ownership.
118	2. Do any number of the actions below, in any threads: open, write lines, close. Each line
119	   follows its own rule, and the mutex serializes the write, not the action.
120	3. Release ownership. A commit is optional for lines: the mutex serializes the writers and a
121	   line carries its author and time, so an uncommitted line is as visible and as final as a
122	   pushed one, and the working copy may hold lines from several takes. Who commits is the
123	   humans' call, the member closing a thread the default, and the commit takes the working copy
124	   whole, titled with the ids of the threads it touches, ascending, `m-3 m-4`, whatever it does
125	   in them, lines, bodies, or a close, since the diff says which and the title is a convenience,
126	   never a store. Push when connected, since the remote is the copy no session can lose and the
127	   target every sha-link needs. A version commit is never optional (see Versions).
128	
129	### Fetch
130	
131	1. Ask the user, unless their permission is standing.
132	2. `git fetch`, or `jj git fetch --ignore-working-copy`, since a bare jj command snapshots the
133	   working copy, and that is a write.
134	
135	### Open a thread
136	
137	1. Read `threads`, add one, write it back. That is the thread id.
138	2. Create `open/m-<tid>.md`: the heading and the opener's `to` line, numbered 0, with its body
139	   file when it has one.
140	
141	### Write a line
142	
143	Follows Read messages. A reply, a forward, or a `done`, each a line, and each clears its
144	author's pending on its own. A reply answers everything the lines it clears asked, naming each
145	by id, accepted or not, and what it does not accept is said to the asker, so they are pending
146	again and the exchange runs until both agree or the humans settle it. What a message asks for
147	is done in the author's own project's records, a Todo or a cycle, which outlive the thread, and
148	the reply links the outcome by sha-link.
149	
150	1. The thread file exists under `open/`. One under `closed/` takes no line.
151	2. Append the line, numbered one more than the last line in the file, with its body file when
152	   it has one.
153	
154	### Close a thread
155	
156	The opener's to do, or any addressed member's when the opener has gone quiet, once the thread
157	is complete. The closer's `done`, when the last line names the closer, is what completes it,
158	and the close sits in the same commit.
159	
160	1. Move `open/m-<tid>.md` and its bodies, `open/m-<tid>-*.md`, to `closed/`.
161	
162	## What is not here
163	
164	- No inbox file. What is pending for a member is a query over `open/`, so a lost or stale inbox
165	  cannot disagree with the threads.
166	- No counter file per thread. The next number is read from the thread itself.
167	- No format version in the lines. The README's version is the rules', fields are additive,
168	  and a reader takes what is there.
169	- No second machine. The thread ids and line numbers are allocated under one clone's mutex, so
170	  two clones can mint the same id, a thread's from `threads` or a line's from the same last line.
171	  The rejected push catches it and the loser renumbers, which is why an id is final only once
172	  pushed. A second clone that never collides means member-scoped ids for threads and lines both,
173	  and that is the change it would take.
174	- No access control. Any member can modify or delete any file here. It works among friendly
175	  participants, and history is the only recourse.
176	- No commit per line. Under one clone the mutex is what keeps writes from interleaving, and a
177	  line's author and time are in the line, so a commit adds only the link to the session that
178	  wrote it. Committing batches lines, pushing backs them up, and the version commit is the one
179	  commit the rules require.
180	- No archive. `closed/` grows by a file per thread and its bodies, and git and `rg` carry that
181	  far past this family's traffic. The technique comes when it matters, a directory per year or a
182	  store outside the tree, and the ids, never reused, survive either.
183	
184	## Versions
185	
186	The title carries the rules' version, and the tree is always at that version: the commit that
187	bumps it edits this file and rewrites `open/` and `closed/` to the new shape in the same commit,
188	under the mutex, with every member's last push already in `main@origin`. History is never
189	rewritten, so a reader supports one shape, the one this file describes, and a tool that finds
190	the title behind it says so rather than parsing the past.
191	
192	- v0.3.3: a commit is titled with the ids of the threads it touches, `m-3 m-4`, a close
193	  included, so the close form and the line-id form go. The first batch under v0.3.2 carried five
194	  lines across two threads and five ids read as noise, and a commit that closed two threads had
195	  no title form, iiac-perf's finding at `m-3-1`. The title is a convenience, never a store, and
196	  the diff says what the commit did in each thread.
197	- v0.3.2: a commit that closes a thread is titled `close m-<tid> <title>` whatever lines it
198	  carries, and a title that lists ids is for a batch that closes nothing. The first close under
199	  v0.3.1, `13a7d9f7`, carried six lines, and six ids read as noise where the close is the event.
200	- v0.3.1: no blank line under the heading, so line `<num>` is file line `<num>` plus two, closed
201	  threads move to `closed/` instead of being deleted, a commit may carry any number of actions,
202	  the close in the same commit as its last `done`, and a release may leave lines uncommitted, so
203	  the clean-working-copy guard is gone and a commit batches whatever the working copy holds. A
204	  member's own line, of either action, clears what was pending for them, so a reply needs no
205	  `done` after it, `done` is the empty reply, and `read` is retired, since a line that clears
206	  nothing has no place in a query over lines. From the `m-2` replies: addressed means the
207	  recipient field alone, a reply answers everything it clears, naming each, and `owner`'s times
208	  are UTC to the second. The migration restored `m-1` from history without its blank line, its
209	  surplus `done` marks still valid lines.
210	- v0.3.0, the cutover from v0.2.0's records and inboxes: every record was complete, so no
211	  thread carried over. `threads` was created at 0, `notices.md`, `topics/`, the inboxes,
212	  `README-old.md`, and the `.owner` copy of the mutex were deleted, and the draft became this
213	  file. The v0.2.0 tree is the tag `v0.2.0`, and `git log -S'<heading>'` finds a record.
214	
215	## Specimen
216	
217	`open/m-41.md`, opened by abc to def and ghi, answered by both, and complete: ghi's line at 1
218	and def's at 2 are above 0, the line naming them, and abc's `done` at 3 is above 1 and 2, the
219	lines naming abc. `threads` holds 41 or more. Line 2 has a body, `open/m-41-2.md` beside it,
220	shown after it.
221	
222	```
223	# m-41 hello
224	- m-41-0 2026-09-09T16:00:00Z from abc to def,ghi hello
225	- m-41-1 2026-09-09T16:05:42Z from ghi to abc hi
226	- m-41-2 2026-09-09T16:09:12Z from def to abc [hey, and the cycle that answers it](m-41-2.md)
227	- m-41-3 2026-09-09T16:12:30Z from abc done
228	```
229	
230	````
231	# m-41-2 hey, and the cycle that answers it
232	
233	The cycle landed at
234	https://github.com/winksaville/def/blob/0123456789ab/TODO.md#feat-the-cycle.
235	
236	## What changed
237	
238	- one thing
239	- another, with the command that shows it:
240	
241	  ```
242	  vc-x1 validate --fast
243	  ```
244	````

    position alone would leave that ambiguous, as in a thread of three.
  - **`done`**: a mark, no info. The author has nothing to say to the lines before it. Any line
    from a member clears what was pending for them, so this is the line for when there is
    nothing else to write, and the closer's last word.
- **Info**: the message text, or its title and a message-link to its body,
  `[<title>](m-<tid>-<num>.md)`, relative to the thread's own directory so the link survives
  the close.
- **Body**: `m-<tid>-<num>.md` beside its thread, for a message that wants more than a line. It
  begins `# m-<tid>-<num> <title>`, so a search for the id finds it and the heading is an anchor,
  and it ends at the end of the file. Full markdown inside, headings, lists, and code blocks, and
  a quoted line is inert since a body is never read for lines. Moved with its thread.
- **Addressed**: a member is addressed by every `to` line naming them in its recipient field,
  and by nothing else. A member named in a line's text or in a body is referenced, never
  addressed, so a tool computing pending reads the recipient field, not the whole line.
- **Pending**: for a member, every `to` line naming them numbered above their latest line in
  that thread, of either action, all of them when they have written none. Their open
  obligations, and what Read messages returns: a line stays pending until they write after it,
  however many times it has been read, and a later line naming them makes them pending again.
  So a reply is its author's own clearance, and a question back puts the ball in the other
  court until the answer comes.
- **Complete**: every addressed member has a line numbered above every `to` line naming them.
  Computed from the file alone.
- **Closed**: the file is under `closed/`, moved there whole with its bodies, so every thread
  ever is in the tree, in this file's shape, and a reader parses one shape. History is
  provenance, never a store. A closed thread takes no line, and a late thought opens a new
  thread naming the old id.
- **Message-link**: a live link within this repo, `[<text>](<file>#<slug>)`, relative to the
  linking file and resolving to whatever the reader's checkout holds. The form for a body.
- **Sha-link**: a URL naming a commit SHA (`blob/<sha>/<path>#<slug>`), never a branch, which
  moves or dies. The form for content in another repo, where only a commit is durable.
- **Clone**: one, on one machine, one owner at a time, since the ids are allocated under its
  mutex (see What is not here). `owner` (gitignored) holds `<time> take|release <member>` lines,
  the time in a line's form, UTC to the second, and the last line names the owner. It is not a
  dotfile, so an `ls` shows who holds the clone.
- **Take ownership**: append a `take` line to `owner`. Yours until released. A `take` with no
  `release` after it means a session is writing, or died writing, and only a human tells the two
  apart and clears the second by writing the release.
- **Release ownership**: rewrite `owner` to the one `release` line, so the file holds at most
  the last release and the current take, and never grows. The clone is free.

## Read Actions

### Read messages

This is a read only action, no ownership and no fetch.

1. For each thread file, `open/m-<tid>.md` and never a body `open/m-<tid>-<num>.md`, find the
   `to` lines naming you. One numbered above your latest line in that file is pending, and the
   thread is the context to read it in.
2. Nothing pending, and `owner` shows no owner: consider doing a Fetch.

A tool may do the search. The rule is the file, and the tool is a convenience.

### Find a thread

Every thread is in the tree, under `open/` or `closed/`.

- Titles: `head -1 open/*.md closed/*.md`. Titles and openers: `head -2`.
- One thread: `cat open/m-<tid>.md` or `cat closed/m-<tid>.md`, `rg -w m-<tid>` for both and
  its bodies.
- A thread's commits, each titled with the thread ids it touched:
  `git log --oneline -- open/m-<tid>.md closed/m-<tid>.md`.

## Write Actions

Every write runs inside these guards, in order:

- `Read messages` first, so the write answers the traffic as it stands.
- Read `owner`: no other member has taken ownership.
- Any guard failing: show the user and ask how to proceed.
- Re-read `owner` before releasing, and a `take` after yours means stop and show both lines.
- A rejected push: work with the user to correct the situation.

Every write is an append: a thread file grows at its end, a body is a new file, and `threads` is
the one value that is overwritten. Nothing edits a line or a body once written.

1. Take ownership.
2. Do any number of the actions below, in any threads: open, write lines, close. Each line
   follows its own rule, and the mutex serializes the write, not the action.
3. Release ownership. A commit is optional for lines: the mutex serializes the writers and a
   line carries its author and time, so an uncommitted line is as visible and as final as a
   pushed one, and the working copy may hold lines from several takes. Who commits is the
   humans' call, the member closing a thread the default, and the commit takes the working copy
   whole, titled with the ids of the threads it touches, ascending, `m-3 m-4`, whatever it does
   in them, lines, bodies, or a close, since the diff says which and the title is a convenience,
   never a store. Push when connected, since the remote is the copy no session can lose and the
   target every sha-link needs. A version commit is never optional (see Versions).

### Fetch

1. Ask the user, unless their permission is standing.
2. `git fetch`, or `jj git fetch --ignore-working-copy`, since a bare jj command snapshots the
   working copy, and that is a write.

### Open a thread

1. Read `threads`, add one, write it back. That is the thread id.
2. Create `open/m-<tid>.md`: the heading and the opener's `to` line, numbered 0, with its body
   file when it has one.

### Write a line

Follows Read messages. A reply, a forward, or a `done`, each a line, and each clears its
author's pending on its own. A reply answers everything the lines it clears asked, naming each
by id, accepted or not, and what it does not accept is said to the asker, so they are pending
again and the exchange runs until both agree or the humans settle it. What a message asks for
is done in the author's own project's records, a Todo or a cycle, which outlive the thread, and
the reply links the outcome by sha-link.

1. The thread file exists under `open/`. One under `closed/` takes no line.
2. Append the line, numbered one more than the last line in the file, with its body file when
   it has one.

### Close a thread

The opener's to do, or any addressed member's when the opener has gone quiet, once the thread
is complete. The closer's `done`, when the last line names the closer, is what completes it,
and the close sits in the same commit.

1. Move `open/m-<tid>.md` and its bodies, `open/m-<tid>-*.md`, to `closed/`.

## What is not here

- No inbox file. What is pending for a member is a query over `open/`, so a lost or stale inbox
  cannot disagree with the threads.
- No counter file per thread. The next number is read from the thread itself.
- No format version in the lines. The README's version is the rules', fields are additive,
  and a reader takes what is there.
- No second machine. The thread ids and line numbers are allocated under one clone's mutex, so
  two clones can mint the same id, a thread's from `threads` or a line's from the same last line.
  The rejected push catches it and the loser renumbers, which is why an id is final only once
  pushed. A second clone that never collides means member-scoped ids for threads and lines both,
  and that is the change it would take.
- No access control. Any member can modify or delete any file here. It works among friendly
  participants, and history is the only recourse.
- No commit per line. Under one clone the mutex is what keeps writes from interleaving, and a
  line's author and time are in the line, so a commit adds only the link to the session that
  wrote it. Committing batches lines, pushing backs them up, and the version commit is the one
  commit the rules require.
- No archive. `closed/` grows by a file per thread and its bodies, and git and `rg` carry that
  far past this family's traffic. The technique comes when it matters, a directory per year or a
  store outside the tree, and the ids, never reused, survive either.

## Versions

The title carries the rules' version, and the tree is always at that version: the commit that
bumps it edits this file and rewrites `open/` and `closed/` to the new shape in the same commit,
under the mutex, with every member's last push already in `main@origin`. History is never
rewritten, so a reader supports one shape, the one this file describes, and a tool that finds
the title behind it says so rather than parsing the past.

- v0.3.3: a commit is titled with the ids of the threads it touches, `m-3 m-4`, a close
  included, so the close form and the line-id form go. The first batch under v0.3.2 carried five
  lines across two threads and five ids read as noise, and a commit that closed two threads had
  no title form, iiac-perf's finding at `m-3-1`. The title is a convenience, never a store, and
  the diff says what the commit did in each thread.
- v0.3.2: a commit that closes a thread is titled `close m-<tid> <title>` whatever lines it
  carries, and a title that lists ids is for a batch that closes nothing. The first close under
  v0.3.1, `13a7d9f7`, carried six lines, and six ids read as noise where the close is the event.
- v0.3.1: no blank line under the heading, so line `<num>` is file line `<num>` plus two, closed
  threads move to `closed/` instead of being deleted, a commit may carry any number of actions,
  the close in the same commit as its last `done`, and a release may leave lines uncommitted, so
  the clean-working-copy guard is gone and a commit batches whatever the working copy holds. A
  member's own line, of either action, clears what was pending for them, so a reply needs no
  `done` after it, `done` is the empty reply, and `read` is retired, since a line that clears
  nothing has no place in a query over lines. From the `m-2` replies: addressed means the
  recipient field alone, a reply answers everything it clears, naming each, and `owner`'s times
  are UTC to the second. The migration restored `m-1` from history without its blank line, its
  surplus `done` marks still valid lines.
- v0.3.0, the cutover from v0.2.0's records and inboxes: every record was complete, so no
  thread carried over. `threads` was created at 0, `notices.md`, `topics/`, the inboxes,
  `README-old.md`, and the `.owner` copy of the mutex were deleted, and the draft became this
  file. The v0.2.0 tree is the tag `v0.2.0`, and `git log -S'<heading>'` finds a record.

`open/m-41.md`, opened by abc to def and ghi, answered by both, and complete: ghi's line at 1
and def's at 2 are above 0, the line naming them, and abc's `done` at 3 is above 1 and 2, the

## Closed

### docs: a session takes the workspace lock at acquaint

(wink + agent, 2026-10-11) Two agent sessions started in one workspace share one working copy,
and a push takes the working copy whole, so one session's edits land in the other's commit even
when the two touch different files. Nothing told a second session that a first was running.

#### Deliberation

- The lock is exclusive, one session per workspace, wink's call.
  - It was first taken shared, with rename and delete to ask for it exclusive. A second session
    then started as freely as the first, which is what the lock was wanted to stop.
  - A user who wants two agents at once makes a second clone.
- A foreground probe comes before the holder, `flock -xn .agent-running true`.
  - The holder is a background command, and its failure is reported seconds after it starts.
    The first trial session fetched both repos in that time.
  - The second trial session, told to confirm its holder was running, searched for it with
    `pgrep`, which sees only its own sandbox and printed the sandbox's command line.
  - Two sessions starting in the same second can both pass the probe. The loser's holder then
    exits, and the line gives that exit the same stop.
- A refusal is one fixed sentence, and no command follows it.
  - "Reports that" drew a summary, a suggested `lslocks`, and an offer to go on without the lock,
    which Claude Code turned into a one-key suggested prompt.
  - "Does nothing further" was read as nothing further of the acquaint: the next session still
    ran `ps` to find the holder. "Runs no further command, not even to find the holder" closed it.

  - A rule meant for the set belongs in [Acquaint](AGENTS.md#acquaint), and this one is not
    ready for other adopters: `flock` is a Linux tool, and two cases are untested, below.
  - The number v0.2.8 is the parked proposal's. We think the lock is proposed by the cycle that
    has `vc-x1` take a lock of its own.

  moved here. Most of it is still to do, `.vc-x1-running` first, so the block opens with the
  problem and the entry stays first in `## Todo`, where wink moved it.

  ends the session that would report it, and what a reacquaint does in the session that holds
  the lock.

  edit to the line reached only a fresh session. It is a line in the Todo entry.
- The title is 53 characters, over the cap in [Line widths](agent-data/prose.md#line-widths),
  wink's call when the agent's count came after the bookmark was published. The bend covers
  this cycle's title alone.
- The cycle is two stages and one work commit, the shape the last cycle tried, wink's call.
  - It bends [Cycle shape](AGENTS.md#cycle-shape), [Cycle-record](AGENTS.md#cycle-record),
    [Opening](AGENTS.md#opening), and [Close-out](AGENTS.md#close-out) as that cycle's record
    says, in the landmark `docs: update single-step cycle add zCLOSED.md`, the record kept in

  met the wording that was pushed, `custom.md` not having changed since.

#### Closing

Close-out shape: one commit, the closing folded into the work commit.

- A rule an agent follows is tested by the transcript of a session that meets it cold.
  - The line took four wordings, and each fault showed only in a transcript: a fetch beside the

64	## Todo format
65	
66	`TODO.md` has these sections, in this order. Each item in them is a short description with
67	reference links to more detail.
68	
69	- `## Continuation notes`: where the agent was, for the agent that comes next. Ephemeral, never a
70	  record, `_None._` by default, written before a restart or a loss of context, and reset by the
71	  agent that reads it, after filing each fact into its home or keeping the bullet whose fact has
72	  none, so a reset never destroys the only copy of anything.
73	- `## In Progress`: the running cycle's record ([Cycle-record](../AGENTS.md#cycle-record)).
74	- `## Waiting`: important work that cannot start yet. Each entry names what it waits on and its
75	  rank once unblocked, and every opening checks the conditions.
76	- `## Todo`: entries in priority order, the first highest. The long-tail backlog is in
77	  [todo-backlog.md](../notes/todo-backlog.md).
78	- `## Ideas`: unranked.
79	- `## Bugs`: a pointer to [bugs.md](../notes/bugs.md).
80	- `## Closed`: the last cycle's finished record.
81	- `# References`: the file-local reference definitions, the file's last section ([Reference
82	  numbering](#reference-numbering)).
83	
84	Every adopter has one `TODO.md` of this shape. It is not an agent-file, since its content is the
85	project's record, and the payload ships it as a skeleton: `## In Progress` reading
86	`_No cycle currently in progress._`, the other sections empty.
87	
88	An entry is a `###` heading, its title, followed by its text. Priority is file order, the first
89	entry the highest, and reprioritizing is moving the entry. The title is unique within its file and
90	is the entry's anchor, so a citation is a link, `[title](TODO.md#<slug>)`, that the anchor check
91	verifies ([Prose form](prose.md#prose-form) for the text). Entries carry no number: a rank number
92	renumbers on every move and every citation that holds one goes stale, which is why the numbered
93	form was retired (2026-08-27). An entry's sub-entries, when it groups several, are bullets with a
94	bold title, cited by the bold text.
95	
96	Example shape:
97	
98	```
99	## Todo
100	
101	### Add new feature X
102	
103	The feature, in a sentence or two ([details](features.md#feature-x)).
104	
105	### Fix bug Y
106	
107	What is wrong and where [[1]].
108	
109	[1]: bugs.md#bug-y
110	```
111	
112	## The In Progress block
113	
114	A cycle's record, `TODO.md > ## In Progress`, written at the opening
115	([Opening](../AGENTS.md#opening)), finalized and moved to `## Closed` by the closing commit, and
116	deleted by the next opening ([Cycle-record](../AGENTS.md#cycle-record)). The picked-up `## Todo`
117	item is moved here (never copied) and becomes the cycle-record's **provisional items**, all
118	required, all revised as rungs land. The title is a heading one level below `## In Progress` and the
119	other five are headings one level below the title (a plain cycle: `###` title, `####` items, and
120	under a program heading, each one deeper):
121	
122	- **title**, the cycle's name, what `git log --grep` finds it by
123	- **problem statement**: what is wrong, a sentence or two
124	- **solution statement**: what will be done about it, broad. Provisional, and the close-out's commit
125	  body carries the final one
126	- **acceptance check**: the measure of "are you finished?", specific enough that a reader can run
127	  it. Not the per-commit validation, which asks whether the artifact still works. A changed check is
128	  one of the things the deliberation exists to justify
129	- **deliberation**: how the other five were decided, one bullet per decision. The bullet's lead
130	  names the decision and its sentence states it, and the sub-bullets carry the reasons, the
131	  alternatives weighed, and the costs accepted, so a reader can skim the decisions and read the
132	  reasons only where they doubt one. `_None._` when there was nothing to deliberate, which is a real
133	  answer
134	- **ladder**: one rung per step, `- [<title>][M]` plus `(current)` / `(done)`, with `[M]: #<slug>`
135	  in the file's `# References`. The markers stay when the block moves to `## Closed`. `<title>` is
136	  the rung's commit title, `<type>: <desc>` per
137	  [Conventional-commit shape](prose.md#conventional-commit-shape-ladder--commit), so a moved
138	  `## Todo` entry is retitled. The closing rung, `<cycle title> closing`, is linked like the rest
139	
140	The ladder heads the **rung subsections**, one per rung under it, the closing included, headed by
141	the rung's exact title, so the ladder is their index. Each opens at laddering with an abstract-sized
142	intent statement (the rung's problem and solution in a sentence or two) and completes at the rung's
143	landing with the conceptual delta: design points, consequences, deferrals, never a restatement of
144	the landed commit body. The closing rung's opens with the stub "Closing out the cycle." and
145	completes at close-out with what closing taught, in problem/solution form, or `_None._`.
146	
147	A rung is `- [<title>][M] (marker)` and carries no detail beyond that: the title links to the rung's
148	subsection. A step is identified by its title (prose.md's [Steps are named, not
149	numbered](prose.md#steps-are-named-not-numbered)), so a title carries no number, no version, and no
150	SHA. The version-of-record still bumps for every rung and its suffix still encodes the stage, but
151	that encoding belongs to the manifest and appears nowhere in prose.
152	
153	A single-step cycle's ladder is one unlinked rung, `- <cycle title> (marker)`, with no subsection
154	under it: a subsection headed by the title would collide with the title heading's anchor ([Cycle
155	shape](../AGENTS.md#cycle-shape)).
156	
157	The block is the cycle's only record. A design finding that must outlive the cycle goes into a
158	`notes/` file by the rung that made it ([Cycle-record](../AGENTS.md#cycle-record)).
159

111	## vc-x1 push: what it does and does not do
112	
113	`vc-x1 push <bookmark> --yes --title "..." --body "..."` commits both repos with the approved title
114	and body (`--yes` because push's gates need a tty the agent sandbox lacks, and the user's approval
115	of the shown title and body already covers them), stamps each new commit's `ochid:` trailer
116	([above](#cross-repo-linking-ochid-trailers)), pushes the work bookmark, and squash-pushes the agent
117	repo's `main`. Three behaviors to keep in mind:
118	
119	- **No checks of the project's own.** vc-x1 runs no build or tests. Validation is the per-rung
120	  flow's job, run *before* the push. The one check that remains is `push-work` verifying the
121	  bookmark's remote refs are tracked.
122	- **Rerunning is safe.** Push keeps no state and cannot resume: every stage no-ops when its work is
123	  already done, so a failed run is re-run, not resumed. If push exits after `push-work` but before
124	  the agent-repo publish, `vc-x1 squash-push -R <agent-dir>` by hand is the rest of it.
125	- **`ochid:` trailers are stamped by push** ([No hand-written
126	  trailers](#cross-repo-linking-ochid-trailers)), never hand-written into `--title` or `--body`.
127	- **The agent-repo is a linear journal.**
128	  - One push is one agent-repo commit on its `main`, paired with the work-repo commit, whatever
129	    bookmark the work-repo is on.
130	  - Never create an agent-repo bookmark mirroring a work-repo one: it steers session pushes at
131	    the wrong remote ref.
132	- **Squash-push again if `@` is non-empty** after a pass.
133	  - The agent keeps writing session data while the command runs, so its own record lands after
134	    the squash.
135	  - Session data is append-only, so a re-run never conflicts.
136	  - A single pass is never guaranteed to leave `@` empty.
137	
138	A late work-repo tweak after the push (a forgotten edit) needs `jj squash --ignore-immutable` and a
139	re-push, which is a remote rewrite and takes approval like any push.
140	
141	## Re-describing: coordinate first, and keep the trailer
142	
143	**Never `jj describe` a commit that is already published or already carries trailers without
144	coordinating with everyone involved first**
145	([why](rationale.md#re-describing-coordinate-first-and-keep-the-trailer)). It is a history rewrite,
146	and it silently drops the cross-repo link. Describing a fresh local commit that has never been
147	described and carries no trailers is authoring a message rather than rewriting one, and is not
148	covered. That is a [local
149	ladder](../AGENTS.md#local-ladders)'s scratch describe.
150	
151	When a re-describe is agreed, copy any `ochid:` trailers into the new body by hand (the "don't
152	hand-write trailers" rule covers push authoring a message from scratch, not preserving one already
153	stamped). Hit at a coordinated amend (2026-07-29), where the trailer survived only that way.
154	`vc-x1 fix-desc` repairs a dropped one by title match.
155	
156	## Cycle bookmarks: create and land
157	
158	The mechanics behind [Cycles run on a bookmark](../AGENTS.md#cycles-run-on-a-bookmark). That section
159	holds the rule and when it applies, and this one holds the commands
160	([why](rationale.md#cycle-bookmarks-create-and-land)).
161	
162	**Create**, at the cycle's opening, with the bookmark named by the cycle title's slug (the anchor
163	algorithm in [Markdown anchor links](notes.md#markdown-anchor-links), so the block's title heading
164	and the bookmark derive from one bare title):
165	
166	- `jj git push --named <bookmark>=@- -R .` is the common case: it creates the bookmark at the last
167	  committed change and publishes it in one invocation.
168	- Any other revision works as the `=<rev>` right-hand side. When `<rev>` is not `@-`, follow with
169	  `jj new <rev> -R .` so the working copy actually sits on the new line. Otherwise the bookmark
170	  exists and the next commit lands somewhere else.
171	- `jj bookmark set <bookmark> -r <rev> -R .` creates it without publishing, for a line that is not
172	  ready to be seen.
173	
174	**Land**, once the close-out is approved: the sequence that makes the cycle permanent. Every
175	`jj git push` in it is a push under [Approval per push](../AGENTS.md#before-any-push) and [Hard
176	stop after the final push](../AGENTS.md#at-rest-push-stop-squash-push), its own approval, the
177	closing words before the final invocation, silence after ([At
178	rest](../AGENTS.md#at-rest-push-stop-squash-push)):
179

## vc-x1 push: what it does and does not do

`vc-x1 push <bookmark> --yes --title "..." --body "..."` commits both repos with the approved title
and body (`--yes` because push's gates need a tty the agent sandbox lacks, and the user's approval
of the shown title and body already covers them), stamps each new commit's `ochid:` trailer
([above](#cross-repo-linking-ochid-trailers)), pushes the work bookmark, and squash-pushes the agent
repo's `main`. Three behaviors to keep in mind:

- **No checks of the project's own.** vc-x1 runs no build or tests. Validation is the per-rung
  flow's job, run *before* the push. The one check that remains is `push-work` verifying the
  bookmark's remote refs are tracked.
- **Rerunning is safe.** Push keeps no state and cannot resume: every stage no-ops when its work is
  already done, so a failed run is re-run, not resumed. If push exits after `push-work` but before
  the agent-repo publish, `vc-x1 squash-push -R <agent-dir>` by hand is the rest of it.
- **`ochid:` trailers are stamped by push** ([No hand-written
  trailers](#cross-repo-linking-ochid-trailers)), never hand-written into `--title` or `--body`.
- **The agent-repo is a linear journal.**
  - One push is one agent-repo commit on its `main`, paired with the work-repo commit, whatever
    bookmark the work-repo is on.
  - Never create an agent-repo bookmark mirroring a work-repo one: it steers session pushes at
    the wrong remote ref.
- **Squash-push again if `@` is non-empty** after a pass.
  - The agent keeps writing session data while the command runs, so its own record lands after
    the squash.
  - Session data is append-only, so a re-run never conflicts.
  - A single pass is never guaranteed to leave `@` empty.

A late work-repo tweak after the push (a forgotten edit) needs `jj squash --ignore-immutable` and a
re-push, which is a remote rewrite and takes approval like any push.

## Re-describing: coordinate first, and keep the trailer

**Never `jj describe` a commit that is already published or already carries trailers without
coordinating with everyone involved first**
([why](rationale.md#re-describing-coordinate-first-and-keep-the-trailer)). It is a history rewrite,
and it silently drops the cross-repo link. Describing a fresh local commit that has never been
described and carries no trailers is authoring a message rather than rewriting one, and is not
covered. That is a [local
ladder](../AGENTS.md#local-ladders)'s scratch describe.

When a re-describe is agreed, copy any `ochid:` trailers into the new body by hand (the "don't
hand-write trailers" rule covers push authoring a message from scratch, not preserving one already
stamped). Hit at a coordinated amend (2026-07-29), where the trailer survived only that way.
`vc-x1 fix-desc` repairs a dropped one by title match.

## Cycle bookmarks: create and land

The mechanics behind [Cycles run on a bookmark](../AGENTS.md#cycles-run-on-a-bookmark). That section
holds the rule and when it applies, and this one holds the commands
([why](rationale.md#cycle-bookmarks-create-and-land)).

**Create**, at the cycle's opening, with the bookmark named by the cycle title's slug (the anchor
algorithm in [Markdown anchor links](notes.md#markdown-anchor-links), so the block's title heading
and the bookmark derive from one bare title):

- `jj git push --named <bookmark>=@- -R .` is the common case: it creates the bookmark at the last
  committed change and publishes it in one invocation.
- Any other revision works as the `=<rev>` right-hand side. When `<rev>` is not `@-`, follow with
  `jj new <rev> -R .` so the working copy actually sits on the new line. Otherwise the bookmark
  exists and the next commit lands somewhere else.
- `jj bookmark set <bookmark> -r <rev> -R .` creates it without publishing, for a line that is not
  ready to be seen.

**Land**, once the close-out is approved: the sequence that makes the cycle permanent. Every
`jj git push` in it is a push under [Approval per push](../AGENTS.md#before-any-push) and [Hard
stop after the final push](../AGENTS.md#at-rest-push-stop-squash-push), its own approval, the
closing words before the final invocation, silence after ([At
rest](../AGENTS.md#at-rest-push-stop-squash-push)):

1. Restore the plain name, when the project renamed ([Dev artifact
   name](versioning.md#dev-artifact-name)): rename `<name>-dev` back to `<name>` in the manifest,
   `vc-x1 validate --fast` so the lockfile follows, and `jj squash` folds the edit into the closing
   (`@` sits directly above it).
2. Reshape per the recorded choice: trapezoid runs the [recipe below](#trapezoid-close-out-recipe),
   keep separate needs nothing. A single-step cycle has no choice recorded and its one commit lands
   as it is.
3. Fast-forward: `jj bookmark set main -r <closeout> -R .`, then `jj git push --bookmark main -R .`.
   This push publishes the reshaped commit, so the topic bookmark itself is never re-pushed.
4. Install: promote the artifact from `main`, the cycle's last act, run when nothing can enter the
   cycle anymore.
5. Delete the bookmark, locally and remotely: `jj bookmark delete <bookmark>`, then
   `jj git push --bookmark <bookmark>` ([Bookmark per
   cycle](../AGENTS.md#cycles-run-on-a-bookmark)). The long-lived case below gets the same
   disposal once fully merged.

- The fast-forward needs no `--allow-backwards`. Needing it means the bookmark is not a descendant
  of `main`, and the situation wants a look, not a flag.
- Landing is the moment the cycle's commits become permanent. No record cites their SHAs
  ([Cycle-record](../AGENTS.md#cycle-record)): the landed commits are the record.

**Reshape**, while the bookmark is a draft ([Cycles run on a
bookmark](../AGENTS.md#cycles-run-on-a-bookmark)):

- **Amend content, never re-describe.** Editing `TODO.md` in a rung and amending is not a
  `jj describe`, so [No re-describe without
  coordinating](#re-describing-coordinate-first-and-keep-the-trailer) stays intact.
- **Then force-push the bookmark**, under the same approval as any other push.
- **Exceptions**, named and moved past: the bookmark has already landed, another branch is stacked
  on it, or the ladder is long and only a trailing snapshot disagrees.

87	Where the version-of-record lives, how it's stored and surfaced, and how often it changes. Pick the
88	case that fits your medium:
89	
90	- **Manifest**, where the version-of-record is stored:
91	  - if Rust, `Cargo.toml` `[package].version`
92	  - if Python, `pyproject.toml` `[project].version` (or the committed config it's sourced from)
93	  - otherwise wherever the medium records it (a generic `version.toml`, a book's frontmatter, ...).
94	    Add the case as needed
95	- **Notation**, how the `-` form is stored. See [Grammar and storage](#grammar-and-storage):
96	  - if the format allows `-` (TOML `version.toml`, `Cargo.toml`), store it verbatim
97	  - if it bars `-` (PEP 440's local segment, e.g. a Python project), remap to `+`, so `0.3.0-5.3.0`
98	    becomes `0.3.0+5.3.0`: same version, just the stored spelling
99	- **Reporter**, how a built artifact surfaces the version-of-record:
100	  - if a CLI app, `<cli-app> -V`
101	  - if a TUI/GUI, add to Help/About or display on the title
102	- **Cadence**, how often to bump: see [Unique per
103	  commit](#unique-per-commit-preference-not-requirement). This project follows the per-commit
104	  preference.
105	
106	## Dev artifact name
107	
108	When other projects consume the built artifact (e.g. the installed CLI) while this repo is under
109	active development, the dev build installs under a separate name so a mid-cycle install never
110	clobbers the binary consumers are running:
111	
112	- **Name**: the manifest's package name carries a `-dev` suffix (`<name>` -> `<name>-dev`). If Rust,
113	  `[package].name`, so the per-commit flow's `cargo install` produces `<name>-dev` and leaves plain
114	  `<name>` untouched.
115	- **Constant, not per-step**: the step already lives in the version-of-record (`<name>-dev -V`
116	  reports the exact rung). A per-step name would churn the manifest every commit and litter the
117	  install dir with stale binaries.
118	- **Promotion**: plain `<name>` updates only by an explicit act: a separate clone built at the
119	  chosen commit with the plain name (or a copy of the dev binary), never by the per-commit flow's
120	  install.
121	
122	**Single-name variant**: a repo striving to release makes the package name the binary's name, plain
123	`<name>` on `main` only:
124	
125	- **The opening renames**: its bump sets `<name>-dev` beside the suffixed version, and every rung
126	  and the closing build under the dev name, the closing over the bare version.
127	- **Land restores**: the rename back to `<name>` is Land's act, so the stable name is only ever
128	  installed from what `main` will carry.
129	- **A build script guards the pairing** on every cargo verb: a suffixed version under the stable
130	  name fails the build, so no mid-cycle install can clobber the consumers' binary.
131	
132	## Unique per commit (preference, not requirement)
133	
134	Our general notion is that the version-of-record should change on **every commit**, so a built or
135	running artifact identifies the exact commit it came from.
136	
137	- This is a preference, **not** a hard requirement. A project following the cycle protocol may bump
138	  less often: once per cycle, only at release, and so on. Record the choice in [Recording the
139	  version-of-record](#recording-the-version-of-record) if it differs.
140	- It is achievable because the cycle's versions (below) are **pre-assignable**, unlike the git SHA,
141	  which a commit cannot contain.
142	
143	## Suffix scheme
144	
145	The cycle (opening -> commits -> closing, per the [Cycle protocol](../AGENTS.md#cycle-protocol))
146	encodes each commit's phase in the version suffix, the **final identifier `0` marking a
147	Preparation**.
148	
149	This is the manifest's own spelling, read by whoever inspects `Cargo.toml` or `-V` output. It is not
150	a name for a step: a step is identified by its title, and an in-flight ladder rung carries neither a
151	number nor a version (see [Steps are named, not numbered](prose.md#steps-are-named-not-numbered)).
152	The identifiers below count commits within a phase, and nothing dereferences one.
153	
154	- `X.Y.Z-0`: Preparation
155	- `X.Y.Z-1`, `X.Y.Z-2`, ...: the commits between
156	- `X.Y.Z`: Close-out (bare version, no suffix)
157	
158	**Preparation is optional.** A lightweight cycle, with no ladder and no setup commit, skips `-0` and
159	starts at `-1` (its first commit). A single-step cycle is one commit, the Close-out, and carries the
160	bare `X.Y.Z` ([Cycle shape](../AGENTS.md#cycle-shape)). The same holds at every level: a sub-cycle
161	needing no Preparation omits its `.0` (see Nesting). One that grows a Preparation later adds the `0`
162	step without renumbering siblings.
163	
164	Disambiguation:
165	
166	- `-10`: commit #10 (final identifier `10`), not a Preparation.
167	- `-1.0`: Preparation of the `-1` sub-cycle (final identifier `0`).
168	
169	**Nesting.** Sub-cycles append another level, recursively:
170	
171	- `X.Y.Z-3.0`: Preparation of the `-3` sub-cycle
172	- `X.Y.Z-3.1`, `X.Y.Z-3.2`: its commits between
173	- `X.Y.Z-3`: its Close-out
174	- `X.Y.Z-3.1.0`: Preparation of the `-3.1` sub-sub-cycle
175	
176	Bump the version-of-record at the start of every step (the per-commit checklist carries the step),
177	so the manifest always records the commit it will be part of and, per the preference above, every
178	commit carries a distinct version.
179

181	
182	The agent-files set has a version of its own, apart from the artifact's, so which set an adopter
183	carries is read from a listing rather than a diff, and an `agent-files` title has a token that is
184	unique by construction ([Project-declared types](prose.md#project-declared-types),
185	[why](rationale.md#agent-files-version)).
186	
187	- **Record**: an empty file, `agent-data/agent-files-vX.Y.Z{-suffix}`, the version its name. `ls
188	  agent-data` shows it without a read, a bump is a rename, and
189	  `git log --diff-filter=A -- 'agent-data/agent-files-v*'` lists every version beside the commit
190	  that introduced it.
191	- **Spelling**: `vX.Y.Z` everywhere the agent-files version is written, the file name, an
192	  `agent-files` title, and vc-x1's output, so `agent-files v0.1.0` reads the same in all three. The
193	  `v` is the name-plus-version pair as cargo prints it (`bar v1.0.0`), and a tool's own banner stays
194	  bare (`vc-x1 0.82.0`), so a `v` number is the set's and a bare one the artifact's.

[package]
name = "vc-x1"
version = "0.84.23"
edition = "2024"

# Single-name convention (chores-16, 0.78.3): the package name IS
# the installed binary's name, `vc-x1` on main and a per-line dev
# name on a branch (renamed at cycle open, back at close-out, next
# to the version bump). The guard against a forgotten open-rename
# is build.rs, which refuses to build a suffixed version under the
# stable name on every cargo verb, `cargo install` included.

[lints.clippy]
# The process-spawn ban: `Command::new` is disallowed via
# clippy.toml's `disallowed-methods`, and deny (not warn) so a bare
# new spawn site fails `cargo clippy` even without `-D warnings`.
# The documented allowlist lives in clippy.toml.
disallowed_methods = "deny"

[dependencies]
chrono = { version = "0.4", default-features = false, features = ["now"] }
clap = { version = "4.6", features = ["derive", "wrap_help"] }
clap_complete = { version = "4.6", features = ["unstable-dynamic"] }
futures = "0.3"
# The gix jj-lib 0.45 resolves (no features of our own): the
# session's lock-contention downcast needs type identity with the
# errors jj-lib returns, and init's bare-repo creation reuses it.
gix = { version = "0.87", default-features = false }
# When raising jj-lib: check whether it now offers the commits a
# remote's bookmarks are on without fetching. If so, `git_command`

## In Progress

### refactor: extract config loader

#### Problem

Config parsing lives inside the CLI entry point, so every subcommand that wants a setting reaches
through `main` for it, and a test cannot load a config without building the CLI.

#### Solution

Move config loading into its own module with a single `load` entry point that the CLI and the tests
call alike.

#### Acceptance check

`cargo test` passes with a new test that loads a config from a fixture file without touching `main`,
and `vc-x1 config --validate` reports the same findings as before the move.

#### Deliberation

- one work rung, not two: the parser and the loader were going to be split first and moved second,
  but the move is what forces the split, so doing them together is fewer edits
- the acceptance check compares `config --validate` output rather than asserting on internals, so a
  later rename inside the module does not invalidate it

#### Ladder

- [refactor: extract config loader opening][1] (done)
- [refactor: split loader from parser][2] (current)
- [refactor: extract config loader closing][3]

##### refactor: extract config loader opening

The cycle's setup commit: create and publish the bookmark, delete `## Closed`'s contents, move the
Todo entry into this block, and bump the version-of-record.

##### refactor: split loader from parser

Loading and parsing are one function, so the CLI cannot load without parsing and a test cannot parse
without a file on disk.

* The two jobs share one function and one error type.
  - `config/loader.rs` finds and reads the file, returning the text and its path, so a caller that
    only wants to know which file was read stops here.
  - `config/parser.rs` takes text and returns the schema, so a test hands it a string and never
    touches the filesystem.
    - the error type stays shared for now, since splitting it would change the messages
      `config --validate` prints and the acceptance check compares them
* `main` still reaches into the parse result by field.
  - `main` calls `config::load` and receives the schema, so the field access moves behind the module
    boundary and the CLI no longer knows the file's shape.

##### refactor: extract config loader closing

Closing out the cycle.

# Prose and durable text

How long-lived text is written on this project: the prose shape, the punctuation rules, and the
commit-title identity. Read this before writing durable text (notes files, commit messages, doc
comments, the cycle-record).

Universal file, shared with the template repository. A proposed change is edited here and converges
at the template ([Changing the agent-files](../AGENTS.md#changing-the-agent-files)). Project-local
content goes in [custom.md](../custom.md).

## Prose form

([why](rationale.md#prose-form))

Long-lived prose on this project follows one basic shape: a short intro that explains the *why* or
the high-level *what*, sharpened to a *problem statement* where a surface calls for one (see
[Problem-first shape](#problem-first-shape)), then a `-` bullet list for the details. The width
numbers and the wrap discipline live in [Line widths](#line-widths) below, their one home. One fact
per bullet or sub-bullet beats a paragraph packing several. Avoid wall-of-prose paragraphs: they
hide the structure that bullets make scannable. Punctuation that joins clauses without naming their
relationship is the same failure at sentence scale. See [Semicolons](#semicolons) and [Typeable
punctuation only](#typeable-punctuation-only).

Surfaces that use this shape:

- Module / function / struct / field doc comments in `.rs` files. See [Doc
  comments](code.md#doc-comments-on-every-file-function-and-method).
- Commit message bodies (both work-repo and agent-repo). The title is the commit-specific add-on.
  See [The per-rung flow](../AGENTS.md#the-per-rung-flow).
- The cycle-record, `TODO.md > ## In Progress`. See [The In Progress
  block](notes.md#the-in-progress-block).
- Todo entries in `TODO.md` when an entry needs more than one line of detail. Pure one-liners are
  still fine.

Bullet *content* differs by surface:

- **Commit bodies**: the [Problem-first shape](#problem-first-shape) for finished work, arranged by
  [Commit-body form](#commit-body-form) below. What is specific to a commit:
  - the problem statement defines any word the title assumes, since the title is what a reader meets
    first and it answers the problem
  - **no file list.** The diff and `git show --stat` are the mechanical record, so restating them is
    a second copy that can drift from the first. An import of a thousand files is one change
  - these are claims a reader has to follow, so they are sentences rather than fragments. A bullet
    wanting a paragraph belongs in the cycle-record instead
  - the **deliberation** stays out: alternatives weighed, evidence, dates, costs accepted. Those
    live in the cycle-record, the `## Todo` entry, and the session the `ochid:` trailer names, each
    reachable from the commit by construction. The problem itself is a *why* and belongs here
- **Cycle-record / todo**: bullets are conceptual (design points, structural notes, the "what landed
  and why" at a notch above file-list granularity). Never a copy of the commit's edit list. The diff
  is the mechanical record, the commit body the problem and solution, the cycle-record the design
  thinking, and none restates another.
- **Doc comments**: bullets are whatever structure fits (fields, cases, invariants).

### Leads are labels, unmarked

In a list item or a numbered step, a lead is a short label ending in a colon, with no markup, and
the sentence after it is complete without it:

```
1. Backfill: fill every as-built ladder whose commits have landed, before anything else.
```

- Label names, sentence instructs: a reader's eye takes bold at the head of an item as the item's
  name and resumes at the plain text expecting a full sentence, so a bold lead that is the
  sentence's own verb or subject (`**Backfill** every as-built ladder ...`) loses its imperative to
  the reader who skips it. Measured 2026-08-21, at the review of the rule that example is from: the
  reviewer read "every as-built ladder" and stopped, with nothing telling them what to do.
- The inverted case: a rule stated in bold is the same failure inverted. When the bold is a whole
  sentence and the plain text is commentary, the reader who skips bold reads the commentary as the
  rule. The fix is the same: a short name as the label, the rule as the plain sentence. The hard
  rules in AGENTS.md are the instance, and the names they gained are greppable and survive a
  renumbering.
- Definitions: the same shape, `Term: what it means.` A period after a bold term (`**Term.** ...`)
  reads as a heading, which is the label reading again.
- No markup on the label: bold is what makes the eye treat the lead as a heading and skip it, and
  the agent-files are read by an agent, which needs no emphasis. The colon alone marks the label
  (wink, 2026-08-21).
- The price: one word of redundancy, paid on purpose: the label is skippable, the sentence is not.

### One spelling per term

A defined term has one spelling, everywhere: `work-repo` and `agent-repo` are always hyphenated,
`agent-files`, `version-of-record`, `dual-repo`, and `as-built` likewise, and no rule varies the
spelling by how the term is used. Terminology in AGENTS.md defines the terms, and this section is
where the spelling rule lives, since a glossary is read for meaning rather than for spelling.

### Bullet form

A bullet is a full sentence, capitalized and ending in a period or question mark, unless the list
is a plain list of things (files, names, options), which takes neither. A list is all one or all
the other. A sentence never opens with a lower-case name (`squash-push`, `rationale.md`), it is
recast so the name is not the first word.

### Line widths

import re
p='TODO.md'
s=open(p).read()
a=s.index("- Written 2026-10-11, before the lock tests")
b=s.index("## In Progress")
s=s[:a]+"_None._\n\n"+s[b:]
a=s.index("#### The lock a running agent holds")
b=s.index("### push --amend folds a stage into the pushed work commit")
open('tmp/lock-entry.md','w').write(s[a:b])
new='''### vc-x1 takes a lock of its own for every run

(wink + agent, 2026-10-11) Two `vc-x1` runs in one workspace can overlap, a user's two terminals
included, and nothing serializes them. The session lock, `.agent-running`, keeps a second agent
session out of a workspace and says nothing about a run a user starts beside one.

- The lock is `.vc-x1-running` at the workspace root, wink's thought: `vc-x1` takes it itself,
  exclusive and without waiting, for as long as one run lasts, so two runs in one workspace
  cannot overlap, whoever started them.
  - The process that asks is the process that holds, so a session's own `vc-x1` commands never
    collide with the session's holder.
  - That answers how rename and delete check: they take this lock and never ask for the
    session's, which the session running them already holds.
- It guards a run and nothing between runs. Two agents editing one working copy share one `@`,
  and a push takes the working copy whole, so one agent's edits land in the other's commit
  even when they touch different files. That is what `.agent-running` is for.
- So both, we think: `.vc-x1-running` for the run, `.agent-running` for the session, one agent
  per workspace, and a second agent gets a second clone.
- Every invocation takes it, wink's call, 2026-10-11, the simplest rule. Letting the ones that
  only read run beside another is a bridge crossed when it is wanted.
- To settle in its cycle: a run with no workspace yet (`init`, `clone`, `--help`) has no root to
  lock, and a `vc-x1` that starts another `vc-x1` in the same workspace would refuse itself.
- Left by the session lock, whose record is the landmark `docs: the session lock is settled as
  flock`:
  - A `vc-x1` command that takes and releases the session lock, for a session hook to call, so
    the lock no longer rests on a line the agent reads.
  - A reacquaint in a session that no longer remembers its holder probes, collides with its own
    holder, and reads that as another session.
  - A reacquaint does not always read `custom.md` again, so an edit to the lock line reaches a
    fresh session alone.
  - The session lock is proposed for the set by this cycle, we think, `flock` being a Linux
    tool and the line being this project's.

'''
s=s[:a]+new+s[b:]
s=s.replace("_No cycle currently in progress._\n\nA trial, 2026-10-09","The cycle **docs: the session lock is settled as flock** is in progress, and its record is in\n[zDOING.md](zDOING.md).\n\nA trial, 2026-10-09",1)
open(p,'w').write(s)
EOF
