content.text:
The lock result is close to certain in advance, so the test is worth less for the lock than for what else it shows.

**Why the lock will be released:** a `flock` lives in kernel memory, not on disk. Pulling the plug destroys the kernel's memory, so after reboot nothing holds it. The empty `.agent-running` file survives, which is fine, since the file was never the lock. The only setup where a lock outlives a dead machine is a network filesystem, where the server holds it, and this workspace is on a local disk.

**What the test does exercise:**
- **The repos:** jj's operation log and git's objects are written without a forced sync on every step, so a power cut mid-write can leave either repo damaged. That is the real exposure.
- **The session transcript:** the agent-repo's latest data may be truncated, which affects whether `claude --resume` works at all.
- **The resume path, cold:** resuming after the reboot is another run of this cycle's acceptance check.

**So I agree with your order, with two additions:**
1. Push, not just commit: finish the review and push stage one, so the work is on the remote.
2. Run `vc-x1 squash-push -R .agent-session` after it, so the session data is on the remote too.

Then run `sync`, wait a few seconds with nothing running but this idle terminal, and pull the plug. Check any other workspace on the machine for unpushed work first, `vc-x1-messages` included.

**A gentler equivalent:** `echo b | sudo tee /proc/sysrq-trigger` reboots at once with no sync, no unmount and no signal to any process. To the kernel and to the lock it is the same event as losing power, without the small hardware risk of a hard cut to the SSD. If the point is thoroughness about the lock, that covers it; if the point is to say "we really pulled the plug", only the plug does.

**After reboot:** run `flock -xn .agent-running true; echo $?` from a plain terminal, expecting 0. Then run `jj st` in both repos to see they are sane, and then resume this session.

The plain version: the lock cannot survive a power cut because it only exists in memory, so the risk in this test is to the repos and the disk, not the lock. Push everything first, and consider the sysrq reboot if you want the same evidence with less risk.

# Commit model

Two commit bodies from the `config loader` cycle in [cycle-model.md](cycle-model.md), shown as
specimens rather than a skeleton: a work rung's body and a bookend's. Copy the shape, not the
words. The rules are in [Commit-body form](prose.md#commit-body-form).

## A work rung

Title: `refactor: split loader from parser`

```
Config loading and parsing are one function, so the CLI cannot load a
config without parsing it and a test cannot parse one without a file on
disk. The move into its own module is what forces the split.

* The two jobs share one function and one error type.
  - `config::loader` finds and reads the file and returns the text with
    its path, so a caller that only wants to know which file was read
    stops there.
  - `config::parser` takes text and returns the schema, so a test hands
    it a string and never touches the filesystem.
* `main` still reaches into the parse result by field.
  - `main` calls `config::load` and receives the schema, so the field
    access moves behind the module boundary and the CLI no longer knows
    the file's shape.
```

The intro states this commit's problem and defines "split", the word the title assumes. Each `*`
is one facet of it, each `-` under a `*` answers that facet, and nothing names a file that the
diff already lists.

## A bookend

Title: `refactor: extract config loader opening`

```
Opens the cycle "refactor: extract config loader". Its record is the
In Progress block in TODO.md.
```

A bookend resolves no problem of its own, so its body is the intro paragraph alone, naming the
cycle by its title and pointing at its record. The closing's body is the same shape with "Closes".

content.content:
112	### Problem-first shape
113	
114	`## In Progress` cycle blocks, `## Todo` entries, and commit bodies use a sharper form of the same
115	shape: a problem, then how it is answered, then the steps that get there.
116	
117	- **Problem statement** (the why): one or two sentences. Don't pad with intent, don't restate what
118	  follows it.
119	- **Solution statement** (the what/how): what is done about the problem, in broad terms, answering
120	  whatever question the problem statement raises. Surface-specific rules are in [Bullet content
121	  differs by surface](#prose-form) above.
122	- **Plan bullets** (the what/when), the steps. Formality differs by surface:
123	  - In Progress: a committed ladder, one step per commit. See [Conventional-commit
124	    shape](#conventional-commit-shape-ladder--commit) for the per-step title + `(current)` /
125	    `(done)` form.
126	  - Todo entries: rough informal bullets, no numbering, formalized only when the entry is picked up
127	    into a cycle.
128	
129	**Timing decides whether the solution statement is provisional, not whether it is written.** A cycle
130	writes one at Preparation, before the work, and revises it as steps land. The close-out's commit
131	body carries the final one. A `## Todo` entry's is provisional in the same way. Only a commit body's
132	is settled, because a commit is finished by the time it has one. The earlier rule here said a plan
133	was for work not yet done and a solution for work that is, which left a cycle unable to say at its
134	opening what it intended to do.
135	
136	### Commit-body form
137	
138	The specimen is [commit-model.md](commit-model.md). A commit body is the [Problem-first
139	shape](#problem-first-shape) with one addition: a body whose
140	problem has several sub-problems arranges them by a fixed recursion, so a reader knows what any
141	bullet is from its marker and its depth. The earlier statement, "a problem statement then a solution
142	statement, both broad", left that arrangement to taste, and taste converged slowly and separately.
143	
144	- **An intro paragraph states the general problem**, and defines any word the title assumes. It is
145	  mandatory. [Prose form](#prose-form) wants it regardless, and a body opening on a bullet is a body
146	  a `--body` flag can mistake for an option. The problem is *this commit's*, never the cycle's: the
147	  cycle's problem lives in the In Progress block, and a body whose problems outnumber what the diff
148	  resolves is describing something larger than the commit.
149	- **`*` bullets are the problem's facets**: sub-problems that decompose the intro's general problem,
150	  not a grab-bag of unrelated fixes. A body reaching for unrelated problem bullets is usually asking
151	  to be more than one commit.
152	- **`-` bullets are solutions**, and every `-` sits under a `*`, solving that facet. A `-` with no
153	  `*` above it reads as a solution to nothing, so there are no top-level solutions: a solution that
154	  retires every facet at once is written under each, or the facets are one.
155	- **One facet is the trivial commit**: the intro, one `*`, one or more `-` under it. Not a second
156	  form, the general form at its smallest.
157	- **A bookend body is a pointer**: an opening or closing commit resolves no problem of its own, so
158	  its body is the intro paragraph alone, naming the cycle by its title and pointing at its record,
159	  the In Progress block. No `*`, no `-`.
160	
161	**The markers are typed on purpose**: `*` always means problem, `-` always means solution, and the
162	pairing is what a reader counts on: the `-` answers the `*` above it, with no rule to consult. The
163	typing also keeps history greppable (`^\* ` finds every facet, `^ - ` every solution). Bodies are
164	read as plain text, in `jj log` and in terminals, where the markers survive, and if a renderer ever

### Problem-first shape

`## In Progress` cycle blocks, `## Todo` entries, and commit bodies use a sharper form of the same
shape: a problem, then how it is answered, then the steps that get there.

- **Problem statement** (the why): one or two sentences. Don't pad with intent, don't restate what
  follows it.
- **Solution statement** (the what/how): what is done about the problem, in broad terms, answering
  whatever question the problem statement raises. Surface-specific rules are in [Bullet content
  differs by surface](#prose-form) above.
- **Plan bullets** (the what/when), the steps. Formality differs by surface:
  - In Progress: a committed ladder, one step per commit. See [Conventional-commit
    shape](#conventional-commit-shape-ladder--commit) for the per-step title + `(current)` /
    `(done)` form.
  - Todo entries: rough informal bullets, no numbering, formalized only when the entry is picked up
    into a cycle.

**Timing decides whether the solution statement is provisional, not whether it is written.** A cycle
writes one at Preparation, before the work, and revises it as steps land. The close-out's commit
body carries the final one. A `## Todo` entry's is provisional in the same way. Only a commit body's
is settled, because a commit is finished by the time it has one. The earlier rule here said a plan
was for work not yet done and a solution for work that is, which left a cycle unable to say at its
opening what it intended to do.

### Commit-body form

The specimen is [commit-model.md](commit-model.md). A commit body is the [Problem-first
shape](#problem-first-shape) with one addition: a body whose
problem has several sub-problems arranges them by a fixed recursion, so a reader knows what any
bullet is from its marker and its depth. The earlier statement, "a problem statement then a solution
statement, both broad", left that arrangement to taste, and taste converged slowly and separately.

- **An intro paragraph states the general problem**, and defines any word the title assumes. It is
  mandatory. [Prose form](#prose-form) wants it regardless, and a body opening on a bullet is a body
  a `--body` flag can mistake for an option. The problem is *this commit's*, never the cycle's: the
  cycle's problem lives in the In Progress block, and a body whose problems outnumber what the diff
  resolves is describing something larger than the commit.
- **`*` bullets are the problem's facets**: sub-problems that decompose the intro's general problem,
  not a grab-bag of unrelated fixes. A body reaching for unrelated problem bullets is usually asking
  to be more than one commit.
- **`-` bullets are solutions**, and every `-` sits under a `*`, solving that facet. A `-` with no
  `*` above it reads as a solution to nothing, so there are no top-level solutions: a solution that
  retires every facet at once is written under each, or the facets are one.
- **One facet is the trivial commit**: the intro, one `*`, one or more `-` under it. Not a second
  form, the general form at its smallest.
- **A bookend body is a pointer**: an opening or closing commit resolves no problem of its own, so
  its body is the intro paragraph alone, naming the cycle by its title and pointing at its record,
  the In Progress block. No `*`, no `-`.

**The markers are typed on purpose**: `*` always means problem, `-` always means solution, and the
pairing is what a reader counts on: the `-` answers the `*` above it, with no rule to consult. The
typing also keeps history greppable (`^\* ` finds every facet, `^ - ` every solution). Bodies are
read as plain text, in `jj log` and in terminals, where the markers survive, and if a renderer ever
flattens them the indentation still carries the structure. So the mixed markers are deliberate, and
a linter's consistent-marker rule is wrong to normalize them.

[Conventional-commit shape](#conventional-commit-shape-ladder--commit).

above). The shared template:

```

  - <optional item>

```

- **Ladder step** (`TODO.md` `## In Progress`): the rung is `- [<title>][M] (marker)`: the title

# Doing: the cycle record

What is being done: the running cycle's planning and its work's documentation. The last
finished cycle's is in [zCLOSED.md](zCLOSED.md), and what we might do is in [TODO.md](TODO.md). The
block's shape is on trial: it opens with the Todo as it was picked from `TODO.md`, then the
Deliberation, the plan, Solution and Acceptance check, and the Ladder with its details.

This file is a trial (2026-10-09). The agent-files still name `TODO.md > ## In Progress` as the
record's home, and the cycle that makes this file the rule is [The cycle-record moves out of
TODO.md into zDOING.md](TODO.md#the-cycle-record-moves-out-of-todomd-into-zdoingmd).

## Continuation notes

Where the agent was, for the agent that comes next. Ephemeral, never a record: read first, acted
on, and reset to `_None._` by the reader. Kept here by the trial, with a pointer to it under the
same heading in `TODO.md`, where [Acquaint](AGENTS.md#acquaint) still looks.

_None._

## In Progress

### docs: the session lock is settled as flock

(wink + agent, 2026-10-11) The Todo as it was picked, **The lock a running agent holds**, less
its plan for `.vc-x1-running`, which stays in `## Todo` as an entry of its own. The file is
`.agent-running` at the workspace root, in `.gitignore`. It is a mutex a running agent holds, one
session per workspace, and a second session that finds it held refuses to work. The entry ended
on an open line: whether the lock is a counter, the `flock`, or a counter guarded by one.

- Wink's first design: the file holds a counter, a session adds one and takes one away, and the
  file is deleted at 0.
  - The update is a read, change, and write that two sessions starting together can interleave,
    so it wants a guard.
  - A session that dies never takes its one away, and a number does not say which holder is dead.
- Linux's advisory lock, `flock`, answers both: the kernel releases it when its holder exits or
  dies. The file then has no contents and is never deleted.
  - The first form was shared: each session held it shared, and rename and delete asked for it
    exclusive without waiting. A second session then started as freely as the first.
  - Wink's call, 2026-10-11: one session per workspace. The session holds it exclusive and asks
    without waiting, so a second session's request fails at once instead of queueing.
  - It is advisory: it binds the processes that ask. Claude Code itself still starts, and the
    refusal is the agent's, by the `custom.md` line.
  - The lock lasts as long as the process holding it, and an agent's commands each exit at once,
    so a session needs one process that lives exactly as long as it does.
- The experiment: the agent takes the lock at acquaint, by a line in this project's `custom.md`,
  which [Acquaint](AGENTS.md#acquaint) already reads and acts on.
  - The holder is a background command the agent starts, `flock -xn .agent-running sleep
    infinity`, so there is no release for the agent to forget.
  - A foreground probe comes first, `flock -xn .agent-running true`, since a background command
    reports its failure seconds later, after the session has moved on.
  - A refusal is one fixed sentence, so the session offers no way around the lock.
  - The check is `flock -xn .agent-running true` from another terminal: it fails while a session
    is open and succeeds after.
- What the experiment was to find out: whether the holder dies with its session, what a resumed
  session does, what a reacquaint does in a session that no longer remembers its holder, how an
  edit to the line reaches a session already open, and how rename and delete check.

#### Deliberation

- The lock is the `flock`, exclusive, and no counter, wink's call once the tests were in.
  - Every way a session ends releases it, so nothing is left for a counter to count.
  - The tests came before the cycle was opened, wink's call, each of them ending the session
    that would have reported it.
- The holder dies with its session, however the session ends.
  - A clean exit: a session was ended with `/exit`, and the next session's probe succeeded.
    Claude Code asks before that exit, the holder being a background command still running, and
    exiting anyway kills it. The question is one more key at every exit.
  - A crash: wink's check from a plain terminal exited 1 with a session open, Claude Code was
    killed with `kill -9`, and the check exited 0 twenty seconds later.
  - A closed terminal: the check exited 1 with the session open and 0 after its terminal
    window was closed.
  - Each session ran its commands in Claude Code's sandbox. One run outside it is untested, and
    we think it is the same, the kernel releasing a lock when the last process holding it dies.
- A resumed session holds no lock, and the line now tells it to take one.
  - The session the closed terminal ended was resumed with `claude --resume`, and the check
    from a plain terminal still exited 0.
  - Claude Code tells the resumed session that its holder was stopped when the earlier process
    exited, and starts nothing in its place.
  - The line as it was gave that case the refusal sentence and the stop, the holder having
    exited, and the sentence would have been untrue, no other session holding the lock.
  - The session ran no command until wink said to take the lock again.
  - "If that command ever exits" became "exits while the session runs", so the two cases do not
    read as one.
- The probe run by the session that holds the lock exits 1, confirmed by running it.
  - A reacquaint in a session that no longer remembers its holder would read that as another
    session and stop. The line's "a session that already holds one does neither" is all that
    stands against it, and the case goes to the `.vc-x1-running` entry with the hook command.
- The link at the end of the lock line is dropped, the entry it named being this record.
- The `.vc-x1-running` plan is an entry of its own, first in `## Todo`, wink's call.
  - It takes what the session lock leaves: the hook command, the reacquaint cases, and the
    proposal of the lock to the set.
  - It answers how rename and delete check, the process that asks being the process that
    holds.
- The cycle is two stages and one work commit, wink's call, as the last two cycles ran.
  - It bends [Cycle shape](AGENTS.md#cycle-shape), [Cycle-record](AGENTS.md#cycle-record),
    [Opening](AGENTS.md#opening), and [Close-out](AGENTS.md#close-out) as the record in the
    landmark `docs: update single-step cycle add zCLOSED.md` says, the record kept in this file
    included.
  - The fold of the closing into the work commit is by hand again, `push --amend` not being
    written, and is a coordinated re-describe with one trailer written by hand.
  - The bend covers this cycle's two pushes and their shape. Land takes its own go.
- The title was counted before the bookmark was published, 42 characters, and both were
  approved by wink at the opening.
- The `## Waiting` conditions are unmet, `vc-x1 closed` not landed and jj-lib offering no remote
  query, so nothing promotes.

#### Solution

Provisional: the session lock is recorded as finished, and what is left is planned elsewhere.

- The lock line in `custom.md` loses its link and gains the resumed session's case.
- The Todo entry becomes this record, with the four results and `flock`, exclusive, as the
  answer to its open line.
- The `.vc-x1-running` plan stands alone as the first entry in `## Todo`.

#### Acceptance check

- `vc-x1 validate` passes.
- A session that met the new line cold takes the lock again when resumed: a fresh session is
  started and acquaints, its terminal is closed, it is resumed and sent one message, and its
  transcript shows the probe and the holder as its first two commands. The check from a plain
  terminal then exits 1.
